name: Yusuf Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Yusuf. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Anything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the city, out of what we call the North Yard. Our crew looks after the older suburbs, where you've got a mix of overhead lines on the back streets and underground cable under the main roads. Lately it's mostly replacing old cable that's sixty years old and starting to fail, so we dig, we pull, we joint, and then we do the overhead where the trees grow into the wires. Thirty-two years I've been doing this, and I still get a little nervous every time we switch a line back on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew. We've been together a long time, we eat together in the van, we know each other's families. What wears me out is the night call-outs in winter, and the traffic, honestly, sometimes we spend an hour getting across the city to a job that takes twenty minutes.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Elif keeps the house and cooks for half the mosque when there's a wedding or a funeral. Our daughter Ayşe teaches primary school, our son Emre is an accountant, and our youngest, Kerem, is twenty-four and an apprentice lineworker at the same company. I put in a word for him, I'm proud of that. We have some savings, a few months, and I'd like to stop at sixty-five with the pension and see my grandchildren more.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. Emre showed me how to ask it questions about the safety rulebook, which is five hundred pages, and it's useful for that. I also used it to help with my speech for Ayşe's wedding, but don't tell her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, like the cable locator was when it came in. It finds the right page in the rulebook, it helps with a letter. But nobody at the yard ever thought a computer would joint a cable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things go the way I planned. I work seven more years, Kerem finishes his apprenticeship and gets his ticket, and I hand over to him, in a way. That's the best picture for my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Keep saving the bit we save each month. Help Kerem with his jointing, he's still a bit rough on the heat-shrink. Maybe help Emre's kids with their school fees a little, if they need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful. Like everything is in its place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hand over to Kerem in a way. What does that mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father fixed tractors in the village, and I didn't follow him, I came to the city. So it means a lot that my son wanted to do what I do. Last month we were on the same job for a day, a cable fault on Station Road, and the foreman put him with me. I didn't say much, but I went home and told Elif about it for an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the usual things. My back, the cold, whether the company keeps hiring enough young people. We're short-handed already, and if they don't train enough apprentices, the old ones work longer nights.

S0.say: I'd call it a useful tool, like the cable locator when it came in. It finds the right page in the rulebook and helps with letters, but nobody thought it would joint a cable.
S0.think: Privately it means everything goes as planned: seven more years of work while my son finishes his apprenticeship. It's the best picture for my family.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving the same small amount each month. Coaches his son on cable jointing and may help with his grandchildren's school costs.
S0.feel: Peaceful, with a sense that everything is in its place.
S0.quote: I didn't say much, but I went home and told Elif about it for an hour.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf's world centres on his son Kerem following him into the trade, which raises the stakes of every later scenario. He treats AI as a modest tool he uses occasionally, much like past equipment changes. His calm here is about continuity for the family, not only his own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company has the right to run its business how it wants, and if the new tools make the network safer, good. But I'd also say they need to keep training apprentices, because a machine doesn't know these old streets. I'd say that to the foreman, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think I'm fine, I'm close enough to the end. For Kerem I'm less sure. If the planning and the fault-finding get done by computer, maybe they need fewer people in the trucks, and the young ones are cheapest to let go or not to take on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the other crews do first. If the new tools work for them, I'll learn them, I'm not proud. And I'd sit down with Kerem and push him to get the extra high-voltage jointing certificate as soon as he can, because the most skilled people are the last to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little worried, mostly for my son. Not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch the other crews first. Has that served you before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the tablets came in, the South Yard got them six months before us. Half their crew hated them, half loved them, and by the time ours came I knew which buttons not to press. My friend Halil in the South Yard called me every week to complain. I learned from his mistakes and never had to make my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kerem, if he asked whether he chose the wrong trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him no. People will always need power, and somebody has to put it in the ground and keep it there. But I'd tell him to be the best on his crew, not the average, because average is what they replace. I'm average myself, I know it, but I had the luck to be born earlier.

S1.say: I'd say the company has the right to run its business as it likes, and safer tools are good. But I'd politely tell the foreman they must keep training apprentices, because machines don't know these old streets.
S1.think: Privately I think I'm fine because I'm near the end. I'm less sure about my son, because if computers do the planning and fault-finding, the young ones are the cheapest to drop.
S1.do: Waits to see how new tools work for other crews before learning them himself. Pushes his son to get an extra high-voltage jointing certificate as soon as possible.
S1.feel: A little worried, mostly for his son rather than himself.
S1.quote: Be the best on his crew, not the average, because average is what they replace.
S1.fieldNote: Yusuf respects the company's right to change but draws a firm line at apprenticeships, which fits his traditional view. His method is to let other crews test new tools first, and he has a story to show it works. He is candid that he is only average himself and was simply born earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should trust God and keep working, and that a robot will take a long time to learn what's under these streets. I'd say it at the mosque too, when the men talk after Friday prayers. But I'd be saying it partly to calm myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's very bad. I'd be sixty, Kerem would be twenty-six and barely qualified, and both our pay comes from the same company. If they decide robots are cheaper, they cut the old ones and the new ones in the same year. Two incomes from one family, gone together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut back hard, no holiday to see my brother, no new kitchen Elif wants. Every extra bit goes into savings. I'd tell Kerem to wait on buying a flat and keep living at home for now, and save his money too. And once I saw the first crew trained on the robots, I'd ask to go on that course, even at sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightening. I'd lie awake thinking I brought my son into a trade that disappeared under him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a heavy thought. Can you tell me more about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When he finished school he wanted to go to college for computers, and I said, no, learn a trade, a trade is safe, nobody can take it from you. He listened to me. If the robots come in two years, then he'd have been better following his own idea. I don't know how I'd look at him at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd lean on savings. What happens if those run out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the family holds together. Ayşe and Emre have good jobs for now, teaching and accounting, though maybe those go too, I don't know. In my culture the children look after the parents and the parents look after the children. I would not want to go to the government with my hand out, but I'd take my son's help without shame.

S2.say: I'd say we should trust God and keep working, and that a robot will take a long time to learn what's under these streets. I'd say it after Friday prayers too, partly to calm myself.
S2.think: Privately I think it's very bad, because my son and I both earn from the same company. If robots are cheaper, the old and the new workers could be cut in the same year, and two family incomes go together.
S2.do: Cuts back hard, dropping a family trip and a new kitchen, and saves every extra bit. Tells his son to delay buying a flat and stay at home, and asks to join robot training once he sees the first crew trained.
S2.feel: Frightened, and haunted by guilt that he steered his son into a trade that could vanish.
S2.quote: Two incomes from one family, gone together.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline threatens Yusuf twice, through his own job and his son's, both at the same employer. His guilt about advising Kerem away from computer studies is the emotional core of the interview. He would still follow others into retraining rather than lead, and he relies on family rather than the state as the safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for sensible people to prepare. I'd tell the young ones at the yard to learn the new machines when they come, and the old ones to save. Like the steady picture, but more serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's much better than two years. I'd be sixty-three, nearly at the pension, and I've seen other crews go first on new things and learned from them. For Kerem, five years means he'd be fully qualified with some experience, and he'd have time to move toward the robot side if he's smart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch for the first robot trials, probably in another yard, and ask Halil how it goes like I did with the tablets. When it's proven I'd take the training, even for my last two years. We'd save more steadily, maybe two hundred extra a month, and I'd make sure Kerem gets every certificate he can before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried in the background. Not like the fast one. More like knowing winter is coming and you've got time to fix the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your advice to Kerem in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd tell him the trade is still good, but he should learn the machines that do the trade. Maybe he goes and studies the computer side at night school, the thing he wanted at eighteen. It would be a little like admitting I was wrong, and that's not easy for a father, but it would be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And once it actually arrives in 2031, what's your day like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be the old man who knows where the cable runs and why it was laid that way in 1965. The robot can dig, but someone has to tell it there's a gas main the drawings missed. I'd do that for two years and then go home to my garden. If they don't want me for that, I'd go early at sixty-three and we'd manage on less.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time for sensible people to prepare. I'd tell the young ones to learn the new machines and the older ones to save, like the steady picture but more serious.
S3.think: Privately I think it's much better than two years, because I'd be sixty-three and near my pension. My son would be qualified and have time to move toward the robot side.
S3.do: Watches robot trials in other depots and checks in with a friend there before taking the training himself once it's proven. Saves about two hundred extra a month and helps his son gather certificates and consider night school in computing.
S3.feel: A background worry, like knowing winter is coming with time to fix the roof.
S3.quote: It would be a little like admitting I was wrong, and that's not easy for a father, but it would be right.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Yusuf room to use his usual method: let others prove a new tool, then follow. The bigger shift is in his advice to his son, which he openly links to admitting he was wrong. His idea of his own value is the knowledge of old cable routes and hidden hazards that the drawings miss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll be drinking tea in my garden by then, God willing. And I'd say the young people have ten years, that's a whole career change if they start early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For my work, almost nothing. I'd retire at sixty-five like I planned, three years before. But Kerem would be thirty-four, maybe married with a baby, and that's the age where losing your trade hurts the most. So it's still on my mind, just not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and saving the way we do now. I'd encourage Kerem to start the computer study in the next few years, while he's young and has no children, so by 2036 he's on the side that runs the machines. And I'd talk to Elif about helping him with a deposit for a flat, so he isn't stuck with rent if things go badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for me, a little uneasy for him. Mostly I'd feel there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be preparing people for this, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First the family, then the company. The company took my son as an apprentice, so they should help him move to the new work, that's fair, he's given them his young years. I don't think the government is good at this, they'd make a scheme with a website and nobody would understand it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you picture the North Yard in 2036, what do you see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer vans, I think, and quieter. Machines in a row charging on the wall. Maybe Kerem with a tablet in his hand, telling three of them where to dig. I hope he still eats lunch with somebody, that's the part I'd miss most if I were him.

S4.say: I'd say I'll be drinking tea in my garden by then, God willing. I'd tell young people that ten years is a whole career change if they start early.
S4.think: Privately I think it barely touches my own work since I'd retire at sixty-five. But my son would be thirty-four, perhaps with a baby, which is the age when losing a trade hurts most.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving as now. Encourages his son to start computer studies in the next few years and discusses with his wife helping the son with a flat deposit.
S4.feel: Calm for himself and slightly uneasy for his son, with a sense that there is time.
S4.quote: Maybe Kerem with a tablet in his hand, telling three of them where to dig.
S4.fieldNote: Even with a decade, Yusuf's worry never fully leaves because it is anchored in his son's future, not his own. He sees family first and the employer second as the ones who should help, and is openly sceptical of government schemes. His closing image of a quiet yard and his son eating lunch alone says what he values about the work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Not only for me, for Kerem, because we'd both go at once and I'd carry the blame for putting him there. What would help is the company promising that apprentices they've taken on get trained on the new machines first, before anyone outside. They made a promise to those young people when they hired them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the crew. People think this job is wires, but it's six men in a van who trust each other with their lives. If the machines come, I hope somebody remembers that you need to trust the one holding the other end.

headlineQuote: I'd lie awake thinking I brought my son into a trade that disappeared under him.
portrait: Yusuf Yilmaz is a fifty-eight-year-old city lineworker who replaces old underground cable and overhead lines from the North Yard, with a homemaker wife, three grown children and a son, Kerem, apprenticed at the same company. He uses AI now and then, waits for other crews to prove new tools, and believes in work, family and faith over government help. He is calm when nothing changes and uneasy about steady change, mostly for Kerem. The two-year AGI picture alarms him because both his and his son's incomes come from one employer, and he feels guilty for steering Kerem into the trade. With five or ten years he plans to follow others into retraining and pushes his son toward the computer side he once talked him out of.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because he and his son would lose their jobs at once and he would blame himself for putting his son in the trade.
whatWouldHelp: The company promising that its own apprentices are trained on the new machines first, before anyone from outside.
